final.format: 3) Never again (reverse psychology: 9 things good hands never do)
final.title: 9 Things Good Hands Never Do
final.stakes: Stakes: if a teacher thinks a good adjustment means pushing a student deeper, students start to fear hands, hold their breath, say yes when they mean no, and quietly stop coming. The teacher loses the students who would have stayed for years. If a student thinks deeper is better, they chase the shape and never learn what safe, skilled help feels like, or that they can always say no.
final.why_care: Why care: teachers who adjust (the 180K audience) decide with their hands who comes back tomorrow. This is the same skill as the 180K pitch: how to build students who stay for years. Students (the Bangkok office worker, the home practitioner in China) will get hands on them in any Mysore room. These 9 tell them what good help feels like and that the choice is always theirs.

slides.text: A good adjustment never pushes. Do you hold your breath when the teacher walks over?
slides.photo_hint: The calmest adjustment photo in the set: one light hand on a student's back in a forward fold, the student's face soft and the breath easy. Pick a beginner or an elder if possible. PUSH sits on empty wall or floor at the top or bottom edge, never on faces, hands or feet.

slides.text: Never put hands on a student before you ask. A yes yesterday is not a yes today. The student can always say no, and no needs no reason.
slides.photo_hint: The teacher kneels beside the student before a twist or drop back, talking or with one hand just resting. The student's face is visible and relaxed. Shows a check-in, not a grab.

slides.text: Never go past the breath. When the breath gets short or stops, the hands stop too. They wait there until it is easy again.
slides.photo_hint: A forward fold (Paschimottanasana) or a deep backbend with the teacher's hand resting still on the back. The student's chest or belly shows easy breathing and the face is calm.

slides.text: Never use more than a light hand. Force can make the body tighten and fight back. Light hands show the way, and the student does the work.
slides.photo_hint: A twist (Marichyasana or Pasasana) with the teacher's fingertips at the shoulder or back. Clearly gentle contact, no leaning or body weight.
slides.source: none (AYBKK teaching content; 'can make' is a teaching view, not a body-science claim)

slides.text: Never chase the shape. A deep asana can sit on a weak base. The legs press and the spine lifts first, then the shape comes. Function over shape.
slides.photo_hint: A backbend (Urdhva Dhanurasana or a drop back) with the teacher's hands at the hips or thighs, so the help goes to the base, not the curve. Feet rooted and in frame, text kept off the feet.
slides.source: none (AYBKK teaching content; 'function over shape' is Boonchu's own method name, the only method name used in this carousel)

slides.text: Never help too late. After the move, a hand can only remind. During the move, it shows the body this part, this way.
slides.photo_hint: A handstand or lift-off, with the teacher's fingertips touching the hips just as the student rises. A moment-of-action photo. Keep text off the space that shows the body leaving the floor.
slides.source: none (AYBKK teaching content; the idea behind 'drawing the cortical map', name not used)

slides.text: Never adjust every body the same way. Same asana, different hips, different day. The hands read this body, this morning, then decide.
slides.photo_hint: A forward fold or wide-leg fold (Prasarita, Upavistha Konasana) with the teacher's hands placed for this body. Better still, a room shot with two students in the same asana looking different and the teacher helping one.

slides.text: Never rush the release. In a drop back, letting go too fast can scare the student. Let go slowly, with the breath, until their own legs hold them.
slides.photo_hint: A drop back with the teacher holding the student at the waist or hips as the student comes up to standing, the hands just starting to let go. Both faces calm.

slides.text: Never think you are too good for help. Teachers need a teacher too. Nobody can see their own back, not even after many years.
slides.photo_hint: An experienced student in an advanced asana (Kapotasana, an Intermediate backbend or a handstand) getting a light assist. This shows that skilled people get help too.
slides.source: none (Plato edit 6 Nov: gymnast line removed, kept only in carousel 2)

slides.text: Never trade a student's next ten years for one deep asana today. A scared student quietly stops coming. Safe hands bring them back tomorrow, same practice, same time.
slides.photo_hint: A warm, quiet moment: a long-time student, ideally an elder, relaxed or smiling during or just after an assist, in morning light in the shala. Ends on trust, not effort.
slides.source: none (AYBKK promise: same practice, same time, a teacher who notices when you are gone; 'ten years' is a figure of speech, not a statistic)

final.caption:
A good adjustment never pushes.
9 nevers for hands-on help, from 14 years of teaching Ashtanga in Bangkok.
For teachers who adjust, and for students who receive.
Which never would you add as number 10?
#aybkk #ashtanga #ashtangabangkok #boonchutanti #mysorestyle
final.notes:
PHOTOS: this run wrote only the text. No photos were gathered. Boonchu needs to pick 10 adjustment photos (drop backs, backbends, handstands, twists, forward folds), or point to the Drive folder, so they can be matched to the photo hints. Use at most 2 photos of the same student. The cover should show a beginner or an elder. Text never goes on faces, hands or feet. The big word sits on an edge or on empty wall or floor. Adjustment is a consent topic, so make sure every student in these photos is happy to be posted.

BOONCHU TO CONFIRM (every line that states how you teach or what you think):
(a) Cover: 'A good adjustment never pushes. Do you hold your breath when the teacher walks over?' Is 'never pushes' true to how you adjust? If not, use word FORCE and 'A good adjustment never forces.' with the same question. If the cover changes, change caption line 1 to match, because it repeats the cover word for word.
(b) Slide 1: do you ask before every adjustment, every day ('A yes yesterday is not a yes today')? If you check with a nod or a consent card, change sentence 1 to 'Never put hands on a student before you ask or check.' (30 words).
(c) Slide 2: 'When the breath gets short or stops, the hands stop too. They wait there until it is easy again.'
(d) Slide 3: 'Force can make the body tighten and fight back.' This is your teaching view, not a body fact. If you want it stated as a body fact, it needs a checked source and a source credit instead of the series label.
(e) Slide 4: 'The legs press and the spine lifts first, then the shape comes.'
(f) Slide 5: 'After the move, a hand can only remind. During the move, it shows the body this part, this way.'
(g) Slide 6: 'Never adjust every body the same way' and 'The hands read this body, this morning, then decide.' Is this how you work alongside the standard Mysore adjustments?
(h) Slide 7: 'letting go too fast can scare the student' and 'Let go slowly, with the breath, until their own legs hold them.' Does this match how you release a drop back?
(i) Slide 8 is your 4 Oct view (skilled people need experienced hands now and then, like gymnasts and ballet dancers), kept as your comparison, not a fact about athletes. 'Nobody can see their own back' echoes your 'we cannot see ourself'. Your wife is not on the slide. Add her only if you want.
(j) Slide 9: 'A scared student quietly stops coming.' Is this your view? 'Next ten years' is a figure of speech, not a number. Change it to 'a student's years' if you prefer.

EDITOR CHANGES: cover word NEVER changed to PUSH (the idea, not the format word) with a self-check question. Slide 2 uses the fact check's 'Never go past the breath' so it no longer clashes with the cover's 'never pushes', plus the reader check's shorter lines 2-3. Slide 3 softened to 'can make'. Slide 5 rewritten so it stays about hands and drops the unclear 'story' line. Slide 6 now says 'every body' so it is not a dig at teachers who use standard adjustments. Slide 7 now gives the reason. Slide 9 says whose years. 'Exactly' removed from the stakes. REJECTED: the reader check's slide 8 line 'Top gymnasts and ballet dancers still need skilled hands' turns your view into an unchecked fact about athletes. Only its shorter sentence 1 was kept. Also rejected: the reader check's 'Never push past the breath' (it clashes with the cover).

METHOD NAME: only 'function over shape' is used, on slide 4. Slide 5 teaches the cortical-map idea but does not use the name. To use 'drawing the cortical map' instead, cut 'Function over shape.' from slide 4 and end slide 5 with 'We call it drawing the cortical map.' (30 words). Never use both names.

FACTS: there are no studies, numbers or quotes on the slides, so no outside sources were needed and all credits are series labels. The caption's '14 years' is AYBKK's teaching years in Bangkok (an allowed fact), not practice years. Sharath's name is not used. There is no price, website, 'come practice' or link in bio. The caption ends with one question, as the 180K rule asks.

RISK: adjustment posts draw comment threads about forcing and consent. Reply short and with care, and ask one question back. Never argue about or shame other teachers.

Word counts: inner slides are 22 to 29 words. Every big word is 3 to 7 letters and appears in sentence 1.

issues.problem: Contradicts the cover. The cover says 'The best adjustment never pushes', but 'Never push past the breath' suggests pushing is fine up to the breath. A commenter will point out the mismatch on a consent topic.
issues.fix: Change sentence 1 to 'Never go past the breath.' Everything else stays (BREATH is still in sentence 1, 25 words).

issues.problem: 'Force makes the body tighten and fight back.' states how the body works as a fact. It is not an allowed fact, has no source, and is missing from the BOONCHU TO CONFIRM list. 'Makes' is an absolute that invites 'says who?'.
issues.fix: Soften it to 'Force can make the body tighten and fight back.' (27 words) and add it to the BOONCHU TO CONFIRM list as (g). If he wants it stated as a body fact, it needs a checked source and a source credit instead of the series label.

issues.problem: 'Never adjust two bodies the same way' is an absolute that is not literally true, because Mysore teachers use standard adjustments for many asanas. Readers can take it as a dig at teachers who teach the traditional set adjustments (no shaming of other teachers or styles). It is also not on the confirm list.
issues.fix: Change sentence 1 to 'Never adjust every body the same way.' (22 words, SAME stays) and add the slide to the BOONCHU TO CONFIRM list.

issues.problem: 'A cue after the move is only a story.' is unclear in 10-year-old English: 'what story?' The idea (a late cue does not help) gets lost over a fast handstand photo.
issues.fix: Change it to 'A cue after the move is just talk.' (slide is 26 words). It stays a teaching picture with no study claim, and the cortical-map name stays unused.

issues.problem: His 4 Oct view is 'even very skilled people need knowledgeable hands now and then, like gymnasts and ballet dancers'. The slide turns the example into a flat fact about gymnasts and ballet dancers. The team's 4 Oct adjustment-reel check flagged this same move ('his opinion now reads as a general fact about gymnasts and dancers').
issues.fix: Keep his structure: 'Even very skilled people need experienced hands now and then, like gymnasts and ballet dancers.' (slide is 28 words).

issues.problem: The BOONCHU TO CONFIRM list says it covers the teaching lines that are not allowed facts, but it skips slide 1. 'Never put hands on a student before you ask. A yes yesterday is not a yes today.' is a public promise that he asks every student every day. The photos of him adjusting will be judged against it. The list also skips slides 3, 5 and 6. The 4 Oct check set the rule that lines like 'Not push. Show.' about how Boonchu adjusts are used only after he says they are true.
issues.fix: Add items: (g) slide 1: do you ask or check before every adjustment, every day? (h) slide 3 force line, (i) slide 5 late-cue line, (j) slide 6 every-body line. If the cover changes after (a), change caption line 1 to match, because it repeats the cover word for word.

issues.problem: 'The teacher loses exactly the students who would have stayed for years' overstates. 'Exactly' is not a true, checked stake (true stakes only).
issues.fix: Delete 'exactly': 'The teacher loses the students who would have stayed for years.'

issues.problem: NEVER is the format word, not the idea, so in one second the reader sees 'never' but not what the carousel is about. 'It asks first, then it listens' gives the adjustment a voice. That is vague and sounds like AI. Nothing makes the viewer question themselves. Also, 'never pushes you deeper' would clash with the slide 8 photo (a Kapotasana assist), so the flip has to be push vs help, not depth.
issues.fix: Word: PUSH. Text: 'A good adjustment never pushes. Do you hold your breath when the teacher walks over?' Credit: '9 NEVERS · SWIPE'. This is clear (teacher hands, pushing), it flips the belief that adjusting means pushing, and the reader asks 'do I?'. Change caption line 1 to match. Boonchu still confirms (a).

issues.problem: This is the weakest slide. 'Cue' is yoga-teacher talk and reads as a spoken instruction, so it leaves the 'good hands' frame. 'A cue after the move is only a story' is vague and sounds like AI. 'This part, this way' is a riddle without the line before it. A 35-year-old would not get why late is bad.
issues.fix: Word: LATE. Text: 'Never help too late. After the move, a hand can only remind. During the move, it shows the body this part, this way.' (23 words.) It keeps Boonchu's phrase and the cortical-map idea without the name, and it stays about hands.

issues.problem: 'Never rush the release' gives no reason, so it fails 'says who?'. 'Release' is hard for a 10-year-old. 'Stand in their own strength' is poetic filler. 'The student rests their weight in the teacher's hands' may not be how Boonchu holds a drop back (confirm item d).
issues.fix: Word: RELEASE. Text: 'Never rush the release. In a drop back, letting go too fast can scare the student. Let go slowly, with the breath, until their own legs hold them.' (27 words.) Sentence 2 now gives the why. Add 'letting go too fast can scare the student' to Boonchu's confirm list.

issues.problem: 'Breath' appears 4 times in 25 words. 'The breath leads again' is vague. What does 'again' mean, and leads what? It sounds like AI.
issues.fix: Word: BREATH. Text: 'Never push past the breath. When the breath gets short or stops, the hands stop too. They wait there until it is easy again.' (24 words.)

issues.problem: 'Never trade the years' is abstract: whose years, years of what? The strong idea (the habit gap, retention) is lost in the first second.
issues.fix: Word: YEARS. Text: 'Never trade a student's next ten years for one deep asana today. A scared student quietly stops coming. Safe hands bring them back tomorrow, same practice, same time.' (28 words. 'Ten years' is a figure of speech, not a stat.)

issues.problem: This is the only slide that speaks to the person receiving help, not to the hands, so it bends the '9 things good hands never do' frame. 'Even skilled ... experienced hands' is wordy and not 10-year-old English.
issues.fix: Word: HELP. Text: 'Never think you are too good for help. Top gymnasts and ballet dancers still need skilled hands now and then. Nobody can see their own back.' (26 words.) It is shorter and punchier, and 'you' now fits a teacher or a student, so the frame holds.

issues.problem: The slide is strong and stays. But 'A yes yesterday is not a yes today' means asking every day, and that teaching line is not on Boonchu's confirm list. If he uses a nod, a consent card or a check instead of a spoken ask, the slide would claim something he does not do.
issues.fix: Keep the text. Add to BOONCHU TO CONFIRM: '(g) Slide 1: do you ask every day? If you check with a card or a nod, change sentence 1 to: Never put hands on a student before you ask or check.'
